extracted.intended_audience: journalists, fact-checkers, researchers and information professionals working on verification and countering disinformation
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy and practical guidance for identifying, classifying, and responding to different kinds of false, misleading or harmful information encountered in journalistic work and verification. Covers types of information disorder, intent distinctions, motivations, amplification pathways and reporting considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire/Parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Content presented as satire or parody which may confuse audiences when context or cues are missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical content can be deliberately labeled to evade fact-checkers and excuse harm. In a fragmented information ecosystem, audiences may not know a site is satirical; sweeping social feeds remove context and increase confusion. Note that some organisations (e.g., Facebook) chose not to fact-check satire, while fact-checkers like Snopes sometimes do, because the satire label can be used strategically by bad actors. Treat claims from unknown sources with caution even if labelled satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Content where the headline, caption or framing makes claims not supported by the underlying content (clickbait/disconnect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic clickbait technique: sensational headline disconnected from the actual article or content. Poor journalistic practices (e.g., misleading headlines) contribute to information disorder and can amplify false beliefs. Evaluate whether the headline accurately reflects the content and whether internal editorial practices may have created the misleading impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that uses selective presentation (quotes, statistics, cropping) to create a misleading impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes selecting partial segments of quotes, creating statistics that ignore how a data set was created, or cropping photos to frame an event in a particular way. These are longstanding journalistic and political problems; identifying such manipulation requires checking source material, methodology, full quotes and original imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Context
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine imagery or content that is re-shared or framed as if it is new or related to current events when it is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very common, especially during breaking news: old imagery or articles reappear as though they are new. Check timestamps, original publication context, metadata and surrounding reporting to verify whether content is contemporaneous with the claimed event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposter Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that uses the logo, branding or identity of a trusted organisation or person alongside false material to increase credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposter tactics exploit heuristics: people trust content that appears to come from organisations they already trust. Look for mismatches in URLs, design inconsistencies, and verify through official channels before attributing content to a trusted source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulated Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine content that has been tampered with or doctored (e.g., edited video or image manipulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: slowed video of Nancy Pelosi to make her sound drunk. Because manipulation is based on real footage, it can be highly persuasive. Investigate for signs of editing, check original uploads, examine metadata and forensic indicators, and compare to known legitimate sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that is entirely invented — new false social media accounts, wholly made-up articles, or deepfakes created with AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes deepfakes and other synthetic media where audio/video or accounts are manufactured. Verification requires provenance checks, account history, technical forensic checks and cross-source corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent distinctions: misinformation, disinformation, malinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework distinguishing false/genuine content by intent: misinformation (false but shared without intent to harm), disinformation (false and shared with intent to harm), malinformation (genuine content shared to cause harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent matters for classification and response. Disinformation is created and shared by actors hoping to cause financial, reputational, political or physical harm. Misinformation is often shared unknowingly (e.g., during breaking news). Malinformation uses real information but with harmful intent (e.g., leaked emails, revenge porn). Use investigations of origin, actor behaviour and contextual signals to assess intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivations for creating false or misleading content
rubrics_metrics.description: Three main motivations: political, financial and social/psychological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political: foreign/domestic actors attempting to influence elections or policy. Financial: creating sensational content to drive clicks and ad revenue. Social/psychological: actors motivated by causing trouble, testing deception, bullying, or identity signalling. Understanding likely motivation helps prioritize verification, attribution and response strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trumpet of Amplification (coordination lifecycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: How disinformation is coordinated and amplified across platforms: from anonymous fringe spaces, to private groups, to alternative platforms, to mainstream social networks and finally professional media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents often seed material in anonymous forums (4chan, Discord), coordinate in DMs/WhatsApp, move into communities on Gab/Reddit/YouTube, then push into mainstream platforms (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter), where it may be picked up by professional media—either as reportage or debunking—further amplifying it. Track provenance, coordination signals and cross-platform movement to understand and counter amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tipping point for reporting and debunking
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial judgement about when to report or debunk a claim: reporting too early can provide oxygen to a rumor; reporting too late means the claim may have already taken hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working out the tipping point is challenging and varies by location, topic and platform. Journalists should weigh the risk of amplifying unverified content against the harm of leaving it unchallenged. Consider the provenance, potential reach, available verification, and whether debunking will embed the false content (e.g., including the false claim in the debunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language matters: avoid imprecise labels like 'fake news'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of imprecise terms (e.g., 'fake news') obscures complexity and can conflate poor reporting with deliberate deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing everything as disinformation is unhelpful. Precision in terminology (misinformation, disinformation, malinformation; satire; false context, etc.) improves analysis, public understanding and response. Be mindful that audiences may equate 'fake news' with any poor reporting practice; choose words that reflect intent and form of the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel-of-truth vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: The most impactful disinformation often contains a kernel of truth — true elements that are mislabelled, recontextualized or presented as new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because disinformation often builds on genuine facts, it can be especially persuasive. Look for partial truths, reused genuine material presented with false framing, and check original context and dates to detect re-use or re-labelling.
